title: A reduced ring with finitely many minimal primes is normal iff integrally closed in its total ring of fractions
statement: Let $R$ be a reduced commutative ring (no nonzero nilpotent element) with only finitely many minimal prime ideals. Let $S\subset R$ be the set of nonzerodivisors of $R$ and $Q(R)=S^{-1}R$ the total ring of fractions [def-weil-pbc-module-localization], with the injective ring map $R\to Q(R)$, $r\mapsto r/1$. The following are equivalent: (1) $R$ is a normal ring [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]; (2) $R$ is integrally closed in $Q(R)$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]: every element of $Q(R)$ integral over $R$ is of the form $r/1$ with $r\in R$; (3) $R$ is isomorphic to a finite product $R_1\times\dots\times R_n$ of normal domains.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 030C (lemma-characterize-reduced-ring-normal, line 8275), with its proof

proof.text: The total ring of fractions splits at the minimal primes. Let $\mathfrak p_1,\dots,\mathfrak p_n$ be the finitely many minimal primes. In a reduced ring the nonzerodivisors are exactly the elements outside their union [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-zerodivisors-union-minimal-primes], so every denominator becomes a unit in each $R_{\mathfrak p_i}$. The localization map therefore gives $Q(R)\to\prod_iR_{\mathfrak p_i}$. The standard localization-prime correspondence identifies the primes of $Q(R)$ with the primes of $R$ disjoint from the denominators; prime avoidance forces each such prime to be one of the $\mathfrak p_i$. By [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-prime-reduced-localization-field] each $R_{\mathfrak p_i}$ is a field. The localization $Q(R)$ is reduced: if $(r/s)^m=0$, then some nonzerodivisor $u$ kills $r^m$, hence $r^m=0$ and then $r=0$. Therefore the intersection of the finitely many maximal ideals of $Q(R)$ is its nilradical and is zero [lem-weil-pbc-zero-locus-eq-iff-radical-eq]. The product-of-localizations decomposition [lem-weil-pbc-product-of-localizations-at-maximal] identifies the displayed map with an isomorphism. (If $n=0$, then $R=0$ and the assertion is the evident zero-ring case.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 030C proof, using Lemmas Tags 00EW, 02LX, 00EU and the localization-prime correspondence

proof.text: Normality implies integral closedness in the total ring of fractions. If every localization $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a normal domain and $x\in Q(R)$ is integral over $R$, then for every prime $\mathfrak p$ the image of $x$ in $Q(R)_{\mathfrak p}$ lies in the fraction field of the normal domain $R_{\mathfrak p}$ and hence lies in $R_{\mathfrak p}$. Let $I=\{a\in R\mid ax\in R\}$. The local membership just obtained says that $I$ is contained in no prime ideal: for each $\mathfrak p$ some $a\notin\mathfrak p$ lies in $I$. Therefore $I=R$, so $1\in I$ and $x\in R$. This is the argument of [lem-weil-pbc-normal-ring-integrally-closed-total].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 030C proof, implication (1) => (2), via Lemma Tag 034M

proof.text: Assume $R$ is integrally closed in $Q(R)$. Under the isomorphism of step 1, each coordinate idempotent $e_i=(0,\dots,1,\dots,0)$ satisfies the monic equation $T^2-T=0$, so it is integral over $R$ and hence belongs to $R$. Multiplication by the $e_i$ gives a ring isomorphism $R\xrightarrow{\sim}\prod_i e_iR$, with inverse $(r_i)\mapsto\sum_i r_i$, because the $e_i$ are orthogonal and sum to $1$. Each factor $e_iR$ identifies with $R/\mathfrak p_i$, hence is a domain, and its fraction field identifies with $R_{\mathfrak p_i}$ (the latter is a field by [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-prime-reduced-localization-field]).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 030C proof, middle paragraph after the total-fractions decomposition

proof.text: Each factor $e_iR$ is integrally closed in its fraction field. Transport the integral-closedness of $R\subset Q(R)$ through the product isomorphisms of step 3 and the total-fractions isomorphism of step 1. The coordinatewise integral-closure statement [lem-weil-pbc-finite-product-integral-closure] then says that the product is integrally closed exactly when every $e_iR\subset R_{\mathfrak p_i}$ is integrally closed. Since each factor is a domain, it is a normal domain. This proves (2) $\Rightarrow$ (3).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 030C proof, final paragraph, using Lemma Tag 0CY9

proof.text: Finally, (3) implies (1): a finite product of normal domains is a normal ring by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-product-normal], since every prime of a finite product lies in exactly one factor and localization there is the corresponding localization of that factor. The implication (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2) is step 2, so all three conditions are equivalent.

split_report.summary: Split Stacks Algebra Lemma 030C into five steps: total-ring-of-fractions decomposition for a reduced ring with finitely many minimal primes; normal implies integral closedness (034M); idempotent decomposition after integral closedness; coordinatewise integral closure (0CY9); and finite-product normality (0CYA). Existing nodes supply minimal-prime fields, zerodivisors, localization prime correspondence and product of localizations. Three supporting unsplit nodes were created; no Lean declaration was attached.
split_report.blueprint: The three equivalences refine the ring-theoretic normality used through the 06DI strict-henselization assertion in the second proof paragraph of lem-weil-pbc-normal-constant-generic. Step 1 supplies the finite-minimal-prime total-fractions decomposition, Step 2 supplies normality-to-integral-closedness, Steps 3-4 derive normal domains from coordinate idempotents and coordinatewise integral closure, and Step 5 supplies the converse product-normality implication. The whole-blueprint search found no blueprint node with the same statement.
